analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal milk price floor and manages dairy surpluses through farmer assessments, exports, and a producer board.
analysis.headline: Three House committees reported the bill and it sat on the House calendar, but it never received a floor vote before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the federal milk price floor to $12.60 per hundredweight in 1992 and 1993, then step it down through 1995. When government purchases of surplus dairy products were projected to run high, dairy farmers would pay a per-hundredweight assessment, and above seven billion pounds the government would pay reduced prices only for milk marketed above each farmer's historical base. A board of producer-elected members would manage, export, and donate the surplus, and milk handlers would have to hold payments in trust for farmers until they were paid in full.
analysis.who_benefits: Dairy farmers gain most: a higher, legislated price floor ($12.60 per hundredweight in 1992 and 1993, stepping down to $11.60 by 1995) and a producer-elected board that decides how surplus-driven price reductions are set. Dairy handlers and processors also gain guaranteed manufacturing allowances that ensure plants can pay farmers the support price. Beef, pork, and poultry producers gain safeguards against a flood of slaughtered dairy cattle depressing red meat prices.

how_it_helps.text: Sets milk price supports at $10.10 per hundredweight for 1991, $12.60 for 1992 and 1993, $12.10 for 1994, and $11.60 for 1995, with no support rate below those floors.
Creates a National Dairy Inventory Management Board of seven members nominated by producers, giving dairy farmers a formal role in deciding reduction rates and managing surplus dairy inventory.

Caps annual Commodity Credit Corporation purchases of excess milk at five billion pounds, with anything beyond that made the responsibility of the producer board, limiting taxpayer exposure when surpluses build.
Establishes statutory trusts requiring milk handlers to hold milk, inventories, and payments in trust for unpaid producers until full payment, protecting farmers when a buyer fails.
Directs the Agriculture Department to buy additional red meat in any year dairy-cattle slaughter exceeds normal culling levels, and includes safeguards to protect beef, pork, and poultry prices.
Authorizes offsetting appropriations for WIC, food stamps, and child nutrition programs to cover milk price increases the bill would cause.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers pay higher retail milk prices under the raised support floor — the bill itself authorizes WIC, food stamp, and school lunch funding to offset those increases. Taxpayers fund the price support purchases up to the five-billion-pound cap plus the nutrition offsets. Dairy farmers themselves pay assessments on every hundredweight when government purchases are projected between five and seven billion pounds, and steep reductions on milk above their production base when purchases exceed seven billion.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers, taxpayers, and surplus dairy farmers

drawbacks.text: The higher support price ($12.60 in 1992-93) raises what consumers pay for milk; the bill acknowledges this by authorizing offsetting appropriations for food stamps, WIC, and child nutrition.

The board that sets producer price reductions is composed of producer nominees and is expressly exempted from the Federal Advisory Committee Act, placing a supply-control pricing decision in the hands of the regulated industry with reduced transparency.

The two-tier base system would pay full price only for milk up to a farmer's historical base, and new dairy farmers would get just 75 percent of actual marketings credited during their first twelve months, disadvantaging new entrants.
States that run their own milk price support programs above the federal level would lose federal price supports entirely.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a serious attempt to fix a real problem — taxpayers warehousing surplus butter and cheese while dairy farm incomes swung — by pairing a higher price floor with self-funded assessments and mandatory export of surpluses. But its design makes consumers the funding backstop: the support floor rises above what taxpayers then paid, and the producer board gets significant power over prices with an exemption from normal federal advisory rules. Dairy farmers would have come out ahead on balance; grocery shoppers would have paid more for milk, cushioned only partly by nutrition-program offsets.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared three House committees and was placed on the House's Union Calendar in October 1991, but House leaders never brought it up for a vote before the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Charles Stenholm introduced the bill on July 9, 1991, after the House Agriculture Subcommittee on Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry held hearings on June 18 and marked it up and ordered it reported on June 25, before the bill was formally introduced.
The Department of Agriculture submitted unfavorable executive comment on the bill in July 1991 and again in September.

The House Agriculture Committee reported the bill amended on July 29, 1991, as Part I of H. Rept. 102-173; Chairman de la Garza had obtained unanimous consent to file the report after the normal deadline.
The bill was then referred sequentially to the Education and Labor and Ways and Means Committees, both of which reported it amended on October 17, 1991, as Parts II and III of the same report.
On October 17, 1991, the bill was placed on the Union Calendar (Calendar No. 150); the action record shows no further action before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers and taxpayers are better off that the bill died: the higher milk price floor and its nutrition-program costs never took effect, and the Agriculture Department, which opposed the bill, did not have to administer the new board and inventory program. Dairy farmers gained nothing, keeping the lower support levels then in law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers who avoided higher milk prices

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors at all, and no recorded votes, so the House's partisan divide never registered on this bill.

industries.note: The bill raises the milk price floor to $12.60 per hundredweight and makes producer-elected board members the operators of the federal surplus-management program, locking dairy farmers into the price support system's revenue while they set the reduction rates themselves. The higher floor is paid for by consumers at the grocery store, cushioned by federal nutrition offsets.

Handlers gain guaranteed manufacturing allowances ($1.37 for butter and nonfat dry milk, $1.52 for cheese) that ensure plants can pay farmers the support price, but they take on new statutory trust obligations to hold payments in trust for unpaid producers and pay for milk on receipt.

The bill requires Agriculture Department red meat purchases when dairy-cattle slaughter exceeds normal culling and mandates safeguards in the heifer export program, protecting meat producers from price-depressing herd liquidations at little direct cost to consumers.
